description:
Wesam Saad introduces the person and ministry of the Holy Spirit after concluding the course’s discussion of salvation. Beginning with the Trinity, he explains that the Spirit is God and a person, with mind, affection and will. The study draws together biblical passages about the Spirit’s work in regeneration, conviction and the continuing growth of believers, encouraging listeners to recognise how much they depend on his patient care.

A central distinction concerns baptism with the Spirit and being filled with the Spirit. Saad presents baptism as God’s action in bringing a believer into Christ’s body at conversion. Filling concerns the Spirit’s continuing influence in a believer’s life. He also explains the Spirit’s seal as assurance of the promised inheritance, drawing attention to the security and comfort God gives his people.

The final emphasis is practical and shared. From Ephesians 5, Saad connects being filled with worship, thanksgiving and fellowship. Believers receive encouragement through the gifts the Spirit gives other members of the church. He urges listeners to make themselves available to one another, sharing their gifts and gratefully receiving help, rather than expecting spiritual growth while remaining isolated from the body.

questions.question: Why does Saad describe the Holy Spirit as a person rather than an impersonal force?
questions.answer: He points to personal language about the Spirit and to his mind, emotions and will. The Spirit can be grieved and distributes gifts as he wills. These passages support Saad’s explanation that the Spirit is a divine person, not simply energy or power.

questions.question: How does the study distinguish the Spirit from the Father and the Son?
questions.answer: Saad explains that the three persons share one divine essence and attributes. Their distinction does not mean that the Spirit is less divine. He then considers the particular work entrusted to the Spirit in applying redemption and helping believers grow.

questions.question: What work of the Spirit does the study connect with becoming a Christian?
questions.answer: The discussion identifies regeneration, conviction of sin, righteousness and judgment, and baptism into Christ’s body. Saad places these alongside the Spirit’s continuing work in believers, distinguishing becoming a Christian from the ongoing process of growth.

questions.question: What assurance does the Spirit’s seal provide?
questions.answer: Using Ephesians 1:13–14, Saad explains the seal in terms of ownership, security and a guarantee of the believer’s future inheritance. Its purpose includes comforting Christians and encouraging gratitude and a continuing walk with God.

questions.question: How are baptism with the Spirit and being filled with the Spirit different?
questions.answer: Baptism brings believers into the universal body of Christ when they are born again; Saad rejects an intervening period in which a Christian awaits that membership. Filling concerns being led, controlled and empowered by the Spirit. He distinguishes God’s initiating action in baptism from the command to be filled.

questions.question: How does Ephesians 5 shape Saad’s explanation of being filled with the Spirit?
questions.answer: He draws attention to speaking to one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord and giving thanks. He presents these shared practices as ways believers make themselves available for God’s work, rather than trying to produce spiritual power themselves.

questions.question: Why does Saad emphasise receiving and sharing gifts within the church?
questions.answer: The Spirit gives different gifts to different people for the good of the body. By participating in fellowship, believers receive help through one another and contribute what they have been given. Saad therefore urges availability and generosity with those gifts, warning against treating spiritual growth as an isolated pursuit.
